newsitem.title: ITALY: Anglican woman priest shrugs off Catholic criticism.
newsitem.headline: Anglican woman priest shrugs off Catholic criticism.

text.p: The first Anglican woman to be ordained priest in Rome on Tuesday brushed aside possible criticism from the Roman Catholic church and said she only wanted to serve God and be a good wife, mother and grandmother.

"I don't think I have done anything that hurts anyone," Cecilia Monge Teran de Erazo told Reuters in an interview in her church, Saint Paul's Within-the-Walls, two days after being ordained an Anglican priest in the capital of Roman Catholicism.
"In the same way that I respect them (Catholics), I deserve respect for my decision and the position I have now."
The ordination of Monge, a soft-spoken 43-year-old Ecuadorian who converted from Catholicism in 1980, has unleashed a torrent of interest in Italy which she said had surprised her.
The Vatican had no immediate comment on her ordination.
But the Pope has made clear he views the Anglican Communion's ordination of women priests as an obstacle to Christian unity.

Wearing a black skirt, cardigan, clerical collar and big silver cross, Monge drew the attention of shoppers in a busy Rome street as she posed for photographers holding hands with her husband Juan outside their American Episcopalian Church.
She described her ordination as "a totally normal event -- the culmination of my vocation".
"All I want is to be a true servant of the Lord and then a good wife, a better wife, a good mother and a better grandmother," she said.

Her rise through the Anglican ranks -- she had been a deacon for six years and heard the call to the priesthood five months ago -- is in stark contrast to Pope John Paul's total ban on the ordination of Catholic women priests.
The Pontiff said earlier this year that women deserved a bigger say in their 960-million-member Church. But the Vatican has given his ban on women priests the force of infallibility.

Monge would not be drawn on the divisions between the role of women in religious life -- an issue which church sources expected to come up at a planned meeting between the Archbishop of Canterbury, Dr George Carey, and the Pope in December.
Carey's Church of England is the mother church of the Anglican Communion, which has some 80 million members worldwide.
"We have different doctrines and government (of the church)," Monge said. "The Pope has his own way of running his Church, we can't tell him what he should do."

Monge, who dreamed as a child of becoming a nun but was told by her parents she should study and then have a family, became disillusioned with Catholicism and converted with her husband Juan after meeting an Anglican priest.
"They accepted us as we are," she said. "All I know is that there is only one God, one faith."
The couple, who met on Good Friday a quarter of a century ago and married three days later on Easter Monday, have three children and two grandchildren.

"We're a family who work in a team," she said, adding it would be "marvellous" if her daughter followed in her footsteps. Her son-in-law was already a lay missionary, she said and her youngest son, aged eight, played music in church services.

Both Monge and her husband work closely with Rome's Latin American community. Parishioners greeted her with hugs and kisses as she prepared for an afternoon of social work. One church annexe put up a big poster congratulating her.
